tip_title: Your Home Policy Offers Three Liability Limits. Most People Have the Lowest One.
topic: Personal Liability Coverage - Limit Tiers and Umbrella Handoff
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Home Policy Offers Three Liability Limits. Most People Have the Lowest One.**

Standard homeowners policies typically come with personal liability limits of $100,000, $300,000, or $500,000 — and the one you have right now is probably the one you got by default when you first set up the policy. The difference in premium between those tiers is usually pretty small. The difference in what they cover if someone sues you after an accident at your home? Not small at all. If you need more than $500,000 in liability protection (and a lot of households with real assets do), that's where a personal umbrella policy picks up — usually starting at $1 million in additional coverage.

Not sure which liability limit is sitting on your current policy? Pull up your declarations page and look for the personal liability line — or ask your Peachy agent to walk through it with you.

📖 [Learn more from NerdWallet](https://www.nerdwallet.com/article/insurance/personal-liability-insurance-homeowners)
summary: Covers the three standard personal liability limit tiers ($100k, $300k, $500k) embedded in homeowners policies and the umbrella handoff above $500k — framed as a limit-selection awareness tip rather than the prior 'go find the default number on your declarations page' angle.
scoring_notes: Prior Aug 24 tip told readers to find the number on their declarations page and flagged the $100k default as likely inadequate. This tip takes the next step: here are the actual tiers, here's what separates them, and here's where umbrella enters the picture. Meaningfully different frame. Both East Cobb (78% homeowners, $118k HHI) and Perimeter (55% homeowners, $105k HHI) have meaningful homeowner populations and income levels where liability adequacy is relevant. Lewisville Lake (65% homeowners, $95k HHI, family-heavy) also benefits. NerdWallet is a trusted source per the skill. Evergreen but works fine in September. Timeliness gets a 6 — no strong seasonal hook, but fall is a natural renewal season and the 'check your declarations page' action is always actionable.

tip_title: Fall Open Enrollment Is Coming. If You Got Married This Year, Don't Miss This Window.
topic: Life Insurance - Open Enrollment and Post-Marriage Coverage Review
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Fall Open Enrollment Is Coming. If You Got Married This Year, Don't Miss This Window.**

Most employer health insurance open enrollment periods kick off in October or November — and if you got married in 2026, that window is your cleanest shot at consolidating coverage, adding a spouse to your plan, or switching to whichever plan actually makes more sense for two people now. The other thing most newlyweds miss: life insurance beneficiary designations. You probably updated your health coverage when you got married, but the beneficiary on an old employer life insurance policy or a standalone term policy doesn't update automatically — you have to go in and change it. A marriage is one of the bigger financial events that touches four or five different policies at once, and open enrollment is the annual reminder to make sure they all reflect your actual life.

If you're heading into open enrollment this fall and want to make sure your coverage still makes sense as a couple, your Peachy agent can help you sort through the pieces.

📖 [Learn more from Forbes Advisor](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/life-insurance/life-insurance-for-married-couples/)
summary: Covers fall open enrollment as a time-sensitive prompt for anyone who married in 2026 to consolidate health insurance coverage and update life insurance beneficiary designations — framed around the October/November enrollment calendar rather than the prior June tip's qualifying-life-event-window angle.
scoring_notes: Prior June 18 tip covered marriage as a qualifying life event for mid-year health insurance changes and the general need to consolidate coverage when two households merge. This tip uses a different calendar hook: fall open enrollment approaching in 6-8 weeks, making it the right moment for anyone who married in the last year to take action. The beneficiary-update angle adds a second concrete action item not covered in the June tip. Timeliness is high (8) because open enrollment season is genuinely approaching in September. Relevance is solid across all three newsletters — median ages of 36-42 mean a meaningful share of readers are in active life-building years where marriage and first-time coverage decisions are live. Forbes Advisor is a trusted source per the skill. Repeat subject (marriage + insurance), but new angle clearly stated: open enrollment calendar timing plus beneficiary update, not the qualifying-life-event mid-year window.
